entry.title: Rhubarb & Gooseberry Crumble Sour
entry.content:
This is my latest iteration of this sour. I'm still using up the rather large quantities of frozen fruit I was gifted along with the freezer I used to make my keezer.

This recpie was tweaked in conversation with Gemini to try and get a more biscuity, crumble-like flavour from the grains. I also doubled the amount of fruit I used, to push those flavours front and centre.

Here's the recipe.

I took a 12l keg to a friend's party last week, and the consensus was that this is the best batch so far, which was pleasing to hear! I would still like to emphasise the crumble a little more, so more tweaking is called for.

entry.title: Fairwater Czech Lager
entry.content:
This is basically a repeat of an earlier recipe, this time with NovaLager rather than W34/70, and a simple single step infusion mash, rather than a decoction.

The first time I did it was based on this recipe (I think!) from TMM

Last time I was pleased with it, and I wanted something similar for the hot summer we're having. Slight changes to the hop schedule to last time, to use what I had in stock, but I stuck with traditional noble varieties.

Here's the recipe.

entry.title: ESB
entry.content:
I've made a few variations on the ESB theme over the years. This batch's variation is that I used WHC Saturated yeast - while this isn't a NEIPA (obviously) I have heard that it's a good choice for an English bitter as well.

For some reason my OG was low - 1.048 rather than the target 1.056. Not sure why, possibly I sparged a bit quicker than I do usually. I'll try to remember to take more measurements on my next brew and if I'm low again then I might get an idea of which stage is causing it.

Here's the recipe.

entry.title: Rhubarb & Gooseberry Sour
entry.content:
Part of the bundle I received when getting the old chest freezer from my in-laws for my keezer build was a large quntity of frozen fruit, which is now occupying a large amount of space in our freezers. This is mainly rhubarb, gooseberry, and backcurrants. Sounds like a lot of sour beer will be in this year's brew schedule!

First off, and using a kilo each of rhubarb and gooseberry, is this recipe. I did a 12l batch last year that went down really well, so this is a scale-up to my normal brew length.

Looking back as I'm writing this up, I used a kilo of each in the 12l batch, so I'm not too sure why I didn't scale the fruit up any for this longer brew... silly me.

Here's the recipe.

Updated 2026-05-10: I kegged this a couple of days ago, and it's tasting really good.

entry.title: Fairwater Facets - Noir
entry.content:
I haven't done a BIPA for a few years, so this should make a pleasant change from my usual pale-n-hoppy beers.

When I went to choose the hops for this one I was very surprised to find that I didn't have anything new-worldy enough in stock - I had English hops like Fuggles and EKG, and European noble hops like Saaz, Tettnang, and Hallertau, but that was about it.

So the recipe as saved here is using a mix of Sorachi Ace and Bramling Cross in the boil and whirlpool, and currently has Citra for dry hopping - which remains to be determined, as I need to buy some new bags of hops and I'll pick one when I get to the dry hopping stage.

Hopefully the Bramling Cross will add some notes of dark fruits that should work with the slightly roasty flavours of the BIPA.

Here's the recipe.

entry.title: Water
entry.content:
Water treatment is far too complicated a topic for me to want to attempt to write a blog post about it - there are far better sources of information out there than me! So that's not what this is about. Rather, it's a brief mention of what our water profile is like around here in Reading, Berkshire.

When I started getting a bit more serious about water treatment I put together a reasonable profile using the information from the Thames Water website - you can get a PDF containing most of the info you need. This is the current one for "Reading East"

I plugged the numbers into a water treatment calculator, and went from there. I originally used the one on the Jim's Beer Kit website, but in recent years I've exclusively used the one in BeerSmith (my preferred brewing software). My results have been fine, but I wanted to confirm that the water profile I came up with actually matched what comes out of our tap, so I bought an "Advanced Water Report from Murphy & Son" from The Malt Miller.

The results were:

Calcium
Ca+2		 Magnesium
Mg+2		 Sodium
Na+		 Chloride
Cl		 Sulphate
SO4-2		 Alkalinity
as CaCO3		 pH Nitrate Total Hardness
as CaCO3
111 2 12 31 18 229 7.9 28 336

Table 1: Water profile for Reading, Berkshire, May 2025.

Interestingly, this is pretty close to what I had originally gleaned from the TW report, no more than a few ppm out in any of the values, but it's good to have proper confirmation!

As a comparison, in The Modern Homebrewer, Andy provides the profile he works from at Elusive Brewing, who are only about 7 miles away from our house:

Calcium
Ca+2		 Magnesium
Mg+2		 Sodium
Na+		 Chloride
Cl		 Sulphate
SO4-2		 Bicarbonate
as CaCO3
118 7 21 41 45 343

Table 2: Water profile for Elusive Brewing, Finchampstead, Berkshire, as listed in The Modern Homebrewer.

Pretty similar, though there's more of a difference than I expected, especially given how close my previous numbers based on the TW report were to the values I got back from Murphy's.

Oh, and I remain as confused as ever between Alkalinity, Total Hardness, and Bicarbonate......

entry.title: Fairwater Facets - Harlequin
entry.content:
The Reading Amateur Brewers Q1 2026 competition is to brew a single-hop showcase using Harlequin hops. Judging will be at the Castle Tap on Thursday 9th April, with Ken from Mysterious Brewing and Ricky from Elusive providing the necessary expertise to find our first champion of 2026!

I've gone for a Harlequin variation on my recurring "Fairwater Facets" beer, which is my new name for what started as "Sim Citra". This is my go-to base recipe for a pale and hoppy beer, and with which I use different hops every time.

I had a minor problem with this batch when I was using the dump valve on my fermenter to remove the dry hops - I managed to leave the valve open slighly, so ended up with half my beer on the floor of the garage. I got about 10 litres kegged in the end, so at least I have enough to enter the competition!

Think I might go back to using a hop sock for dry hopping, especially in larger quantities such as this, as I always have a struggle getting the crap to flow out of the dump valve. It always seems to get blocked and is difficult to free.

Here's the recipe.

Update 2026-04-13: I'm still amazed that I can say this, but I won! I had a real problem getting a bottle and growler filled to be able to take to the judging, and consequently the beer was significantly under-carbonated. Luckily for me, Ken and Ricky were able to see past that and award me first place in our Q1 competition.
